author: Tajender Singh Katal
headline: Senior Data Engineer | Databricks | AML | Spark | SQL | Python | Scala | Airflow | DBT | Quantexa | Snowflake | AWS | GCP | Azure & Dataiku Certified Developer
text:
Startup interview Question: (Senior Data Engineer)

I recently had the opportunity to participate in an interview process for a company I was very interested in. As part of the test, I was tasked with building an end-to-end data pipeline and encountered an interesting challenge:

Problem: For each (subscription_id, month) pair, keep only the latest record, without any updated_at or created_at timestamps!

Solution: In Spark, DataFrames are unordered by default, so I used monotonically_increasing_id() to simulate row ordering and identify the “latest” row. I had learned about this function in a Udemy course a while back, and this project gave me the opportunity to actually implement it and see how it works in practice. 😊 

Key Takeaways:

1) Prefer real timestamps whenever possible.
2) monotonically_increasing_id() is a handy fallback but only guarantees order within partitions.
3) Including ingestion timestamps during ETL is the best practice to avoid such issues.
It was a great exercise in thinking creatively about data ordering and pipeline design! 😊

That’s the real gatekeeper.
𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲. 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗛𝘂𝗯. 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗟𝗲𝗲𝘁𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸.

At home, it feels manageable because:
✔️ You Google error messages
✔️ You write code in your favorite IDE
✔️ You pause, restart, and take breaks mid-solve

But in a real interview, here’s how 60 minutes actually go:
⏳ 0–10 mins → Clarify the problem + understand business context
⏳ 10–20 mins → Discuss architecture, edge cases, bottlenecks
⏳ 20–45 mins → Write SQL/Python or design scalable data flows
⏳ 45–60 mins → Optimize, justify decisions, handle follow-ups

Most candidates stumble — not because they lack skills — but because they haven’t practiced the real interview experience.

author: Ajay Kadiyala
headline: Senior Data Engineer @ Emirates NBD | Data & AI Engineering | Azure • Databricks • PySpark • SQL | Data Engineering Mentor | Dubai, UAE
text:
I still remember the day 𝗜 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝘇𝗲 𝗶𝗻 a Data Engineering interview....
Salary on the table: ₹30 LPA.
 The role: Senior Data Engineer.
 The reason I failed: 𝗦𝗤𝗟.

I thought I knew SQL. I’d written 500-line queries in production.
Instead, they asked me questions that tested clarity, not complexity:

1️⃣ Write a query to find the 2nd highest salary without using LIMIT or TOP.
2️⃣ Find customers who purchased in Jan but not in Feb.
3️⃣ Explain indexes—when they speed up queries, and when they actually slow them down.
4️⃣ How would you debug a slow query in a billion-row table?
5️⃣ Why should SQL code be modular instead of one giant query?

By the third question, I was stuck.
45 minutes later, the interview was over.

I learned:
1. SQL is not about writing long queries, it’s about writing clean, efficient, and logical queries.
2. Data Engineering interviews go beyond SQL they test how you think about systems, pipelines, scalability, and quality.
3. Preparing from random YouTube videos wasn’t enough.
